text: The Taliban has released a biography of its reclusive leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, aiming to dispel rumors of his death and reaffirm his leadership. The 11-page document outlines Omar's daily routine and early life, including his founding of the Taliban in the 1990s. The move is seen as an attempt to counter the rise of ISIS and reassert Omar's jihadi credentials.

Hundreds mourn Walter Scott, fatally shot by police, at South Carolina funeral. Scott's death has sparked calls for change and allegations of racial prejudice. Officer Michael Slager faces murder charges in the case.

Former TSA agent sentenced to 6 months in jail for secretly videotaping female coworker in bathroom. Daniel Boykin, 33, pleaded guilty to unlawful photography and burglary after over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of victim were found on his devices. Boykin also received 5.5 years probation with GPS monitoring.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost its economy, with events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo aiming to promote local artists and attract tourism. The country's government and private sector are working together to develop the creative economy, with music seen as a key sector. Cape Verde aims to increase tourism to 20% of GDP by 2024, with its unique musical culture a major draw.

Arsenal kept their Premier League title hopes alive with a 1-0 win over Burnley, moving within four points of leaders Chelsea. The win was Arsenal's eighth in a row, ahead of a crucial matchup against Chelsea next week. Chelsea remain in control with two games in hand, including a Sunday match against Queens Park Rangers.

Twin Peaks original cast members back David Lynch in salary dispute with Showtime. Cast launches #SaveTwinPeaks campaign amid Lynch's exit from revival project. Showtime holds out hope for Lynch's return to the series.

Andrew Getty, 47, heir to the Getty oil fortune, has died of apparent natural causes at his Los Angeles home. A preliminary assessment found no foul play, with Getty having had several health issues and medication recovered from the scene. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the official cause of death.

Maryland police say Nyia Parler, 41, cannot be extradited to Philadelphia to face charges until she completes unspecified treatment. Parler is accused of abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in woods for days while she visited her boyfriend. She will face charges including aggravated assault and reckless endangerment once treatment is complete.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Malala Yousafzai, the Pakistani education activist. The asteroid, 316201 Malala, is approximately 4 kilometers in diameter and orbits the sun every 5.5 years. The naming honors Malala's contributions to girls' education and women's empowerment.

Gastrointestinal illness outbreak affects 100 on Celebrity Infinity cruise ship. CDC investigating cause, sending staffers to meet ship in San Diego. Outbreak is third on ship, which has increased cleaning and disinfection measures.

The "Star Wars" saga is now available on digital HD, actress Mindy Kaling's brother sparked controversy by revealing he posed as a black man to get into medical school, and other notable stories trended this week. Notable deaths included actor James Best, known for his role as Sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane. A Burger King couple scored a free wedding courtesy of the fast food chain.

US authorities charge Philadelphia woman with attempting to join ISIS overseas. Two New York women also arrested on terror charges for allegedly plotting to build an explosive device. The cases bring to over 30 the number of people prosecuted for supporting terrorist groups in the past 18 months.

HBO releases teaser for "True Detective" season 2, starring Colin Farrell and Vince Vaughn, premiering June 21. The new season follows a murder investigation in California involving three law-enforcement officers and a career criminal. The series returns after a critically acclaimed first season that crashed HBO's website with its finale.

A Massachusetts man, Carlos Colina, 32, has been charged in connection with the discovery of human remains in a duffel bag in Cambridge. The remains were identified as those of 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who knew Colina. Colina faces charges of assault and battery and improper disposal of a body.

Trey Moses, a star basketball player, asks Ellie Meredith, a freshman with Down syndrome, to prom in a viral gesture. Moses, a college recruit, was originally planning to take his girlfriend, but instead chose Ellie, citing her kindness and ease to talk to. The prom invitation has drawn widespread praise and attention to the importance of inclusivity.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues", a 12-week miniseries and sequel to the History Channel's "The Bible", on Easter Sunday. The series picks up with Jesus' resurrection and follows the early days of Christianity. Other notable premieres this week include "Mad Men" on AMC and "Marvel's Daredevil" on Netflix.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence faces backlash over signing a religious freedom law that allows discrimination against gays and lesbians. The move is seen as an attempt to boost his conservative credentials ahead of a potential 2016 presidential run. The controversy is expected to drag the Republican field further to the right on LGBT issues.

Apple has released a new version of its mobile operating system featuring more diverse emojis, including various skin tones and same-sex couples. The update has been met with both praise and criticism, with some groups feeling included and others, such as redheads, feeling left out. The move is seen as a step towards greater representation of America's changing demographics.

Avril Lavigne reveals she was bedridden for 5 months due to Lyme disease. The Canadian singer, 30, was bitten by a tick last spring and suffered from undiagnosed symptoms for months. Lavigne is now "80 percent better" and set to release a new single.

New research suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died of typhus at least a month earlier than previously thought, likely before February 1945. The revised timeline is based on archives and survivor testimonies re-examined by the Anne Frank House. Exact dates of death remain unclear.

Two Alabama college students arrested, charged with gang rape of woman at Florida's Panama City Beach during spring break. Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, students at Troy University, face sexual battery charges. Further arrests expected as investigation continues.

A stray dog in Washington State has survived being hit by a car, bludgeoned with a hammer, and buried alive. The dog, named Theia, was found four days later and is receiving care at a veterinary hospital for injuries including a dislocated jaw and leg injuries. Donors have raised over $10,000 to cover her medical expenses.

FBI confirms Malaysian bomb maker Marwan killed in January raid in Philippines. Marwan, a top terrorist suspect, was linked to southeast Asian terror group Jemaah Islamiyah and had a $5 million bounty on his head. The raid that killed him resulted in the deaths of 44 Philippine police officers.

US President Barack Obama's administration has reached a nuclear deal with Iran, but critics argue it gives Tehran too much leverage. The deal allows Iran to maintain its nuclear infrastructure and provides billions in sanctions relief. Critics warn the agreement lacks tough safeguards and could enable Iran to cheat and develop a nuclear bomb.

The final season of "Mad Men" premieres Sunday, marking the end of an era for the 1960s-set drama. The show's creator, Matthew Weiner, has kept the finale under wraps, but it's expected to pick up where the previous season left off, in the late 1960s. The final episodes will likely explore the characters' struggles with change and disintegration as the decade comes to a close.

A giraffe at the Dallas Zoo gave birth to a 6-foot-tall calf during a live internet stream. The hour-long labor was captured by 10 cameras and broadcast by Animal Planet. The newborn's gender and condition have not been announced, but it appeared healthy in initial observations.

Loretta Lynch's nomination for US Attorney General has been delayed for six months, the longest wait in recent history. Democrats claim the delay is due to her race, while Republicans attribute it to partisan battles over other issues. Lynch's confirmation vote remains unscheduled.

Three killed, five wounded in attack on Afghan attorney general's office. Armed assailants stormed the office in Balkh province, sparking ongoing exchange of fire with security forces. Afghan forces are advancing cautiously to minimize civilian casualties.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to host "The Price Is Right" for the first time in eight years. He led the show's first game, "Lucky Seven," before handing over to Drew Carey. Barker's appearance marked a one-day comeback after a 35-year hosting stint that ended in 2007.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, hospitalized for dehydration due to Type II diabetes. King released a statement saying he is "feeling much better" and has been discharged from hospital. He is now resting at home with his grandchildren.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev found guilty on all counts in Boston Marathon bombing trial. Experts say understanding radicalization of young Muslims is key to preventing similar violence. Addressing grievances such as corruption and foreign intervention may help counter extremist narratives.

Former heavyweight champ Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion is set to become a church. A dramatic interview with Bikram yoga creator Bikram Choudhury aired amid allegations of sexual assault. Other notable videos include a tour of the world's tallest "giga-coaster" and an eyewitness account of the Germanwings crash.

Coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory from ISIS, according to a Pentagon map. The gains are seen as significant, but experts warn that ISIS remains adaptable and able to launch asymmetric attacks. The terror group's losses are likely to be offset by attempts to distract from defeats with spectacular attacks elsewhere.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta was allegedly choked by a stranger with a headphone cord. The incident occurred about 30 minutes before landing, and the suspect was escorted off the plane by US authorities. The suspect was taken for medical and mental evaluation, with no federal charges pending.

A Hong Kong court has adjourned the murder case against former banker Rurik Jutting until May. Jutting, 29, is charged with killing two Indonesian women, Seneng Mujiasih and Sumarti Ningsih, whose bodies were found in his apartment last November. The case has shocked the city and sparked outrage over the treatment of migrant workers.

Multiple tornadoes ripped through the rural Midwest, killing one person in Illinois and causing widespread damage. The storms tore through several states, including Illinois, Iowa, and Oklahoma, with several homes destroyed and many more damaged. Despite the severity of the storms, only one fatality has been reported so far.

Don McLean's manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction. The 16-page draft includes handwritten notes and unused lines, offering insight into the song's meaning. The sale is the third-highest price for an American literary manuscript at auction.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl to make emergency visit to Syria's Yarmouk refugee camp amid deepening humanitarian concerns. The camp, under control of armed groups, is home to 18,000 Palestinians and Syrians, including 3,500 children. Krähenbühl will assess the situation and meet with officials and displaced individuals.

Fighting in Yemen has killed an estimated 600 people in under two weeks, with airstrikes and ground battles causing widespread destruction. The International Committee of the Red Cross is calling for a humanitarian ceasefire to allow aid into the country. A Saudi-led coalition is bombing Houthi rebel targets, while the UN Security Council has discussed a draft resolution to halt the airstrikes.

Former Australian cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at 84. Benaud, a veteran of 64 Test matches, was a renowned commentator and player who was inducted into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame in 1985. His passing has sparked an outpouring of tributes from the cricket world and beyond.

A total lunar eclipse occurred this morning, lasting 4 minutes and 43 seconds, visible in western North America. The eclipse was also partially visible across the US and in parts of South America, India, China, and Russia. It is the third in a series of four eclipses, known as a "tetrad".

Robert Durst, 71, charged with unlawful possession of a firearm, faces up to 10 years in prison. The real estate heir is also accused of first-degree murder in California and faces state charges in New Orleans. Durst could face the death penalty if convicted of the murder charge.

Paul Walker's death in 2013 is still being felt as "Furious 7" hits theaters. The film pays tribute to the late actor, with a rewritten script and special effects used to finish his scenes. Walker's co-stars and fans continue to remember him as a kind and humble person.

Model accidentally reveals correct answer on "The Price Is Right", giving away a new car. Host Drew Carey laughed off the mistake, congratulating the contestant on their win. The error occurred on Thursday's edition of the popular game show.

Thai Smile airline unveils Adventure Time-themed Airbus A320. The plane features characters from the show on its exterior and interior. The themed flight is part of a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone water park.

Pedestrians in Washington, DC, intervened to help a mother duck and her brood safely cross a busy street. The group used an umbrella to guide the ducks to a nearby grassy area. The unusual scene unfolded on a rainy street in the city's northwest area.

French investigators have collected all main evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site in the Alps. The site is now being secured by a private firm until remaining debris is removed for further analysis. All 150 people on board were killed in the March 24 crash.

Cuba and the US are set to interact at the Summit of the Americas in Panama, marking a historic shift in relations. The meeting may pave the way for a formal agreement to re-establish diplomatic ties and re-open embassies. The US is also considering removing Cuba from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a key Cuban demand.

Jesus and his disciples likely survived on a subsistence level, relying on donations and hospitality to meet their basic needs. Women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna, who had been healed by Jesus, provided financial support from their own resources. The ministry may have also received substantial donations from wealthy supporters, including men like Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

California regulators have ordered Pacific Gas & Electric Co. to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe operation of its gas transmission system. The penalty, largely in the form of mandated safety improvements, stems from a 2010 pipeline rupture that killed eight people in San Bruno. The fine surpasses the previous record of $146 million.

Lauren Hill, 19, has died after a battle with brain cancer. The Indiana college basketball player inspired millions with her determination and courage, helping to raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research. She will be remembered as a symbol of strength and perseverance.

A large fire broke out at General Electric's Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke into the air. Authorities reported no injuries or entrapments, but the cause of the blaze remains unknown. Firefighters responded to the multi-alarm fire, working to contain the damage.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, key to nuclear talks with US, has received a hero's welcome in Iran. Less well-known facts about Zarif include his education in the US and past involvement in protests at Iranian diplomatic missions. Zarif is set to continue negotiations with US Secretary of State John Kerry to meet a June 30 deadline for a nuclear agreement.

A Connecticut judge has denied a motion to release a 17-year-old girl from state custody, despite her being in remission from Hodgkin lymphoma after forced chemotherapy. The girl, who was diagnosed in September, will remain in custody until her treatment is complete, expected by the end of April. Her attorneys plan to consider further appeal.

Researchers claim to have confirmed that "Double Falsehood", a play published in 1728, was actually written by William Shakespeare and John Fletcher. A study using computer software to analyze language patterns found a strong match between the play and Shakespeare's writing style. The findings may settle a long-standing debate over the play's authorship.

French prosecutor Brice Robin denies knowledge of video footage from Germanwings Flight 9525, despite claims by two magazines of a cell phone video showing the crash's final seconds. The videos were allegedly recovered from a phone at the wreckage site, but investigators say they have not analyzed any cell phones yet. The crash killed all 150 on board.

A federal lawsuit is pending in the DC Circuit on behalf of American Samoans, including veteran Emy Afalava, who are seeking US citizenship despite being born on US soil. The case challenges the government's denial of citizenship to those born in American Samoa, a US territory since 1900. A decision is expected soon.

Blue Bell ice cream has shut down its Oklahoma plant due to listeria contamination found in some products. The company has recalled certain 3-ounce servings made at the plant and warned consumers not to eat them. The recall is linked to a listeria outbreak that has killed three people in Kansas.

Al-Shabaab claims attack on Kenya's Garissa University College, killing many and taking hostages. The attack is part of the group's escalating activities in East Africa, where it has been behind several recent attacks. The security situation in the region continues to deteriorate.

US complains to Russia over "unsafe and unprofessional" intercept of US reconnaissance plane by Russian fighter jet over Baltic Sea. The incident occurred in international airspace, with the US denying Russian claims that the US plane's transponder was switched off. The US will file a formal complaint through diplomatic channels.

A hooded angel statue with black wings has become a symbol of the Black Lives Matter movement after appearing near the site of Walter Scott's fatal shooting in North Charleston, South Carolina. The artwork, created by local resident Phillip Hyman, has been featured at protests and rallies, evoking emotions and sparking conversations about police violence. Hyman crafted the piece as a way to mourn with Scott's family and comment on the state of America today.

North Charleston police Officer Michael Slager has been fired and charged with murder after a bystander's video showed him shooting unarmed black man Walter Scott eight times as he ran away. The video contradicts Slager's initial report that Scott had taken his Taser, with witness Feidin Santana saying he saw no such struggle. Slager now faces murder charges in the death of 50-year-old Scott.

ISIS claims to have seized part of Iraq's largest oil refinery, posting images of clashes and smoke. Iraqi officials deny the claim, insisting they remain in control of the facility. The refinery's fate is unclear, with CNN unable to verify ISIS' assertion.

Nashville's district attorney has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization as part of plea deals, following public outcry over the practice. The move comes after it was revealed that prosecutors had offered sterilization as an option four times in the past five years. The constitutionality of sterilization as punishment remains unclear, but it appears that defendants can voluntarily choose it as part of a plea deal.

Ebola outbreak: Over 25,000 infected, 10,000 dead in past year. New cases persist, with 30 reported in week of April 5, despite decreased intensity. Guinea remains a concern due to unsafe burials and unidentified transmission chains.

NCAA claims no legal responsibility to ensure education of student-athletes, contradicting its public stance. The organization made the claim in response to a lawsuit filed by former University of North Carolina athletes affected by a major academic fraud scandal. Critics call the NCAA's position "nonsense" and "double talk".

Explosion at Chinese chemical plant sparks huge fire, injuring six. The blast occurred at an oil storage facility in Fujian province's Zhangzhou city. Firefighters have brought the blaze under control.

A defense attorney argues that police body cameras could have prevented the fatal shooting of Walter Scott by Officer Michael Slager in North Charleston. The use of body cameras can help reduce use-of-force incidents and increase accountability among law enforcement. Implementing body cameras is seen as a crucial step in addressing racial bias and rebuilding trust between police and the community.

Tensions rise at the VII Summit of the Americas in Panama City as Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro clashes with the US over sanctions and alleged coup plots. Cuba has sided with Venezuela, complicating the highly anticipated meeting between US President Barack Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro. The summit has become a "triangle of tension" between the three nations.

Fire breaks out on Russian nuclear submarine in dry dock at Zvyozdochka shipyard. Insulation caught fire during welding work, but no ammunition or nuclear fuel on board. No injuries reported, fire poses no threat to surrounding area.

Tropical Storm Maysak, known locally as Chedeng, approaches the Philippines with 70mph winds. Authorities warn of flash floods and landslides, taking precautions including evacuations and barring outdoor activities. The storm is expected to make landfall Sunday morning on the southeastern coast of Isabela province.

NFL legend Deion Sanders chastised his son on Twitter for claiming to only eat "hood doughnuts", reminding him of his privileged upbringing. Sanders Jr, a college athlete and entrepreneur, took the public rebuke in stride, retweeting his father's comments. The exchange played out in front of Sanders' 912,000 Twitter followers.

Guatemalan woman survives attempted murder, seeks justice in a country where nearly 10 out of every 100,000 women are killed. Gender-based violence is at epidemic levels in Guatemala, with two women killed daily. Efforts to address the issue are underway, including new laws and programs to support survivors.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring residents to register their cattle with photos and unique identifying features to enforce a state-wide ban on beef sales and consumption. Over 100 owners have complied so far, with the goal of creating a database to track and prevent cow slaughter. The move follows a recent crackdown on cow slaughter in the state of Maharashtra.

Indian police to deploy pepper-spraying drones to control violent crowds. The drones, equipped with cameras and pepper spray, will be used in Lucknow and other cities. The move has sparked concerns over freedom of speech and excessive use of force.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript for "American Pie" has sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction. The 1971 song is a cultural anthem that has become an enduring piece of American pop art. The manuscript's sale marks a new chapter for the iconic song's original lyrics.

A daring heist in London's jewelry district has seen thieves break into a vault and crack open dozens of safety deposit boxes, with the raid bearing similarities to a movie plot. The gang's meticulous planning and old-school methods have drawn comparisons to notorious robberies of the past. Police are investigating the possibility of inside involvement and are analyzing forensic evidence and CCTV footage to track down the culprits.

7-Eleven to host Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, allowing customers to fill unique containers for $1.49. Participating stores will have size and sanitation guidelines in place. The promotion kicks off peak Slurpee season.

Kentucky Senator Rand Paul has launched his presidential campaign despite a record of questioning voting rights and civil rights legislation. Critics say his attempts to rebrand himself as inclusive are at odds with his policies, which they claim are outdated and disqualifying. Paul's announcement was met with skepticism from those who say his views undermine progress made in civil rights over the past five decades.

A Lamborghini crash at Walt Disney World Speedway's Exotic Driving Experience killed a 36-year-old passenger. The driver, 24, lost control and was hospitalized with minor injuries. The incident occurred during a fantasy sports car ride on Sunday.

Aaron Hernandez's defense team has rested its case in his murder trial, with jurors to begin deliberations soon. The former NFL star is accused of killing semi-pro player Odin Lloyd in 2013. The case relies heavily on circumstantial evidence, with prosecutors pointing to inconsistencies in Hernandez's alibi and potential motive.

Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for "creating disturbances" after planning protests against sexual harassment. The activists' fate will be decided by April 13, when they must be either released or formally arrested. The detentions come as China prepares to mark the 20th anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women and considers adopting its first anti-domestic violence law.

Former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley suggests Hillary Clinton's inevitability as Democratic presidential nominee is not guaranteed. O'Malley, a potential contender, cites Clinton's 2008 loss to Barack Obama as an example of an "inevitable" candidate falling short. Clinton is expected to launch her candidacy on Sunday.

Aaron Hernandez sentenced to life in prison for first-degree murder of Odin Lloyd. Lloyd's family members delivered emotional statements in court, remembering him as a devoted family man and gifted athlete. Hernandez, a former pro-football player, will serve his sentence without possibility of parole.

Ted Cruz courts Iowa's evangelical voters as he seeks to propel his presidential campaign forward. Cruz is counting on the state's vocal Christian right to support him in a crowded GOP field. He is emphasizing social issues and his own faith in an effort to energize evangelical voters.

Marvel Studios releases poster of Paul Bettany as the Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron". New images also unveiled for Netflix's "Daredevil" and the "Fantastic Four" reboot. Superhero film trend shows no signs of slowing with new character announcements for "X-Men: Apocalypse" and "Deadpool".

Italian Coast Guard rescues 978 migrants in Mediterranean Sea off Libya. At least 480 migrants have died crossing the Mediterranean this year, often due to bad weather and overcrowding. Migrant arrivals in Italy have surpassed 10,000 in the first three months of 2015.

French TV network TV5Monde regains control of one channel after cyberattack. The network, which broadcasts to 260 million homes worldwide, was crippled by the attack, which included ISIS logos on its social media accounts. TV5Monde is gradually restoring its channels and online presence.

Director David Lynch exits "Twin Peaks" revival over budget disputes. Showtime says it's "saddened" by the decision, but hopes to still bring back the series with Lynch and co-creator Mark Frost. The network will continue with production on the nine-episode third season.

High-profile trials near conclusion in Massachusetts, with jury deliberations set to begin in cases of Aaron Hernandez and Boston bombing suspect Dzhokhar Tsarnaev. Sen. Rand Paul announces presidential bid, while voters head to polls in Chicago mayoral runoff and Ferguson, Missouri, elections. Key verdicts and election outcomes expected today.

Tornadoes reported in Kansas and Missouri as severe storms sweep through the Midwest. Multiple twisters spotted in Kansas, with additional reports of wind damage and flooding in Missouri. Further storms expected Thursday in the region.

Jodi Arias sentenced to life in prison for 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. Arias, 34, expressed remorse before sentencing, saying she was "disgusted" with herself. She will serve her sentence at the Arizona State Prison Complex-Perryville.

A Delaware family of four fell ill at a luxury villa in the US Virgin Islands, with preliminary EPA results showing presence of toxic pesticide methyl bromide. The EPA is investigating whether a fumigation at the resort caused the illness, which has resulted in hospitalization. A criminal investigation has also been initiated by the US Department of Justice.

Rolling Stone has apologized for its discredited article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia, citing "institutional failure" in reporting and editing. The fraternity at the center of the story, Phi Kappa Psi, may pursue defamation claims, but faces hurdles in proving individual harm and meeting strict legal standards. A lawsuit is possible, but its success is uncertain.

FBI agents have captured a suspect in 32 commercial robberies after a shootout in Georgia. Two agents were injured in a crash during the pursuit, but their injuries are not serious. The suspect, Kevone Charleston, was shot and wounded but is expected to survive.

Alaska Airlines flight returns to Seattle after pilot reports banging in cargo hold, where a sleeping ramp agent was found. The agent, who had fallen asleep during loading, was unharmed and passed a drug test. The flight was delayed but later continued to Los Angeles.

A North Carolina judge has ruled that Craig Hicks, accused of killing three Muslim college students, can face the death penalty. Hicks, 46, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the February shootings. The case may also be investigated as a hate crime.

Amnesty International has called on Afghan authorities to protect women's rights activists amid a surge in attacks and killings. The number of women killed in Afghanistan increased by 20% in 2013, with most cases linked to domestic violence and cultural traditions. Activists continue to face persecution despite recent shows of solidarity, including women pallbearers at a high-profile funeral.

A New York judge has authorized serving divorce papers via Facebook private messaging. The ruling allows for electronic service as a means of notifying a defendant of a lawsuit when traditional methods are not possible. The move reflects a shift towards online service as a more reliable and trackable alternative to traditional methods.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" TV ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, has died at 88. Schuller, who was diagnosed with esophageal cancer in 2013, passed away peacefully, according to his family. He was a prominent televangelist known for his upbeat and encouraging message.

Four workers killed, 45 injured in oil rig fire off Mexico's coast. The blaze on Pemex's Abkatun Permanente platform was extinguished after hours. Cause of the fire, which prompted evacuation of 300 people, is unknown.

Kansas enacts first-in-US law banning "dismemberment abortion" procedure. The law, signed by Gov. Sam Brownback, restricts second-term abortions with exceptions for mother's health. Opponents vow to challenge the measure in court.

Chinese TV host Bi Fujian sparks controversy after being filmed cursing late Chairman Mao Zedong at a dinner party. Bi has apologized for his comments, which are considered taboo in China. State-run China Central Television has announced an investigation into the incident.

University of Kentucky basketball player Andrew Harrison apologizes for using a racial slur in reference to Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky after a loss. Harrison claimed his words were "in jest" and meant no disrespect. Kaminsky has accepted Harrison's apology, saying he's "over it".

"Arrested Development" to return for 17-episode fifth season, according to exec producer Brian Grazer. Netflix has not confirmed the report. The quirky comedy previously streamed its fourth season on Netflix in 2013.

The Large Hadron Collider has resumed operation after a two-year shutdown, with beams circulating in its 17-mile ring. The particle accelerator aims to recreate conditions after the Big Bang to uncover new insights into the universe's evolution. Scientists will use the LHC to explore fundamental questions about mass, dark matter, and the universe's composition.

Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a US Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, sparking concern over potential loss of control by Iranian commanders. The incident, which occurred during a routine US patrol, was deemed an unsafe maneuver that could have triggered a serious incident. The US is considering a protest against Iran over the encounter.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev found guilty on all 30 counts in Boston Marathon bombing trial. The 21-year-old faces possible death penalty in upcoming penalty phase. Jury to weigh aggravating and mitigating factors in deciding Tsarnaev's sentence.

Indian police arrest 4 FabIndia employees after federal minister discovers security camera overlooking store changing room. The employees face voyeurism and breach of privacy charges, punishable by up to 3 years in jail. The store has been sealed and the company is cooperating with the investigation.

Iran to lift ban on women attending some sports events, including indoor games, within the next year. The move comes after international pressure, including from FIFA President Sepp Blatter. Details on which specific events will be open to women are still unclear.

Indian court sentences software pioneer Ramalinga Raju to 7 years in jail for role in $1.6B Satyam Computers fraud. Raju, former Satyam chairman, also fined $804,000 for cheating and conspiracy. Nine others also convicted in India's largest corporate scandal.

Alaska Airlines apologizes for removing a cancer patient from a flight due to concerns over her ability to fly without a doctor's note. The woman, Elizabeth Sedway, was eventually rebooked on a later flight and received a refund and compensation for overnight accommodations. The airline acknowledged that while the decision was made with her well-being in mind, it could have been handled differently.

Turkish singer and songwriter Kayahan dies at 66 after long battle with cancer. The musician, known for his love songs, passed away in an Istanbul hospital just days after his birthday. He was a beloved figure in Turkish music, with a career spanning nearly 20 albums.

Israeli PM Netanyahu criticizes Iran nuclear deal, saying it falls short and that increased pressure could yield a better agreement. US politicians remain divided on the deal, with Democrats defending it and Republicans calling for tougher sanctions. Netanyahu's opposition has sparked a backlash from some Democrats, who urge him to "contain himself".

Shootings rock Washington area, linked to domestic kidnapping incident. A guard at the US Census Bureau and a police officer were injured, suspect also wounded. The kidnapping victim was found safe, authorities said.

Imprisoned soldier Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating tweets to a communications firm due to lack of internet access in prison. Manning, serving 35 years for leaking classified documents, has gained over 26,000 followers. She will use the platform to engage in two-way conversations despite her incarceration.

Rapper Nelly arrested in Tennessee on felony drug charges after state trooper stops his tour bus on Interstate 40. Nelly, 40, charged with possession of methamphetamine, marijuana, and drug paraphernalia. He was released from jail after posting bond.

A Delaware family fell ill, possibly due to pesticide exposure, while vacationing in the US Virgin Islands. The father is in stable condition, while his two teenage sons remain critical. The EPA is investigating the incident, which may be linked to the use of methyl bromide at their rented villa.

Governments in Asia are increasingly cracking down on online dissidents, using laws and intimidation to silence critics. Journalists and bloggers in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam face arrest, fines, and even violence for their online activities. The region has seen a surge in attacks on bloggers, with several killed in Bangladesh in recent years.

Nina Dobrev to leave "Vampire Diaries" after sixth season. Fans express outrage and sadness over her departure, citing concerns over the show's future without her character. Dobrev and producers have acknowledged the backlash, with the show set to continue into a seventh season.

Fighting in Syria's Yarmouk camp has intensified after ISIS stormed the area, with government forces responding with bombing and shelling campaigns. Only 18,000 of the camp's original 100,000 residents remain, with many lacking food, water, and medical care. The UN has called for increased aid and protection for civilians trapped in the camp.

NASA scientists discuss steps to discover life elsewhere in the universe, with estimates suggesting 40 billion Earth-like planets in the Milky Way galaxy. The likelihood of finding intelligent life that can communicate with Earth is considered low, but possible signs of life on exoplanets may be detected in the coming decades. NASA's upcoming James Webb Space Telescope will aid in the search for life on rocky, habitable exoplanets.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina, 32, faces murder charges in connection with remains found in Cambridge. The remains, identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, were discovered in a duffel bag and a common area of an apartment building. Colina is to be arraigned on April 14.

Kanye West has settled a lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he assaulted in 2013. The terms of the settlement were not disclosed, but included an apology from West to Ramos. The case was set to go to trial next week before the settlement was reached.

US President Barack Obama's legacy is tied to a nuclear deal with Iran, which has led to a negotiating process influenced by political considerations. The framework agreement announced Thursday allows Iran to keep a significant nuclear capability, sparking concerns among US allies in the Middle East. The deal may not be enough to prevent nuclear proliferation and instability in the region.

A white police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, has been charged with murder after a bystander's video showed him shooting an unarmed black man, Walter Scott. The incident highlights a lack of comprehensive data on police killings, despite a 1994 law requiring the Justice Department to collect such data. The absence of reliable statistics hinders efforts to understand and address potential racial bias and excessive force in policing.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in West Africa have been released from an Omaha hospital after three weeks of monitoring. None developed the virus, and four have returned home while one remains in the area due to a heart issue. The releases come as a larger group of 17 monitored patients are expected to be cleared by Thursday.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars leads the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, becoming the longest-leading single of the 2010s. The song also becomes one of only 10 to top the chart for at least 13 weeks in its history. Newcomer Natalie La Rose reaches the top 10 with her debut hit "Somebody" featuring Jeremih.

Film fans mark dates from iconic movies, including April 8 as "Rex Manning Day" from "Empire Records" and October 21, 2015, as the future date visited in "Back to the Future Part II". Other notable dates include April 14 from "Titanic" and October 3, known as "Mean Girls Day". These dates have become cultural references and are celebrated by fans on social media.

"Grace of Monaco" starring Nicole Kidman will premiere on Lifetime on May 25 after The Weinstein Co. decided against a US theatrical release. The film, which opened the 2014 Cannes Film Festival, was critically panned and performed poorly internationally. It will now bypass theaters and go straight to TV.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward has passed an ordinance allowing same-sex couples to register for "partnership certificates", granting them some rights such as hospital visitation and co-signing tenancy agreements. The move is seen as a step towards marriage equality in socially conservative Japan. The certificates, to be issued later this summer, are not legally binding but a significant development in the country's LGBT rights movement.

California's historic drought, now in its fourth year, is expected to drive up US food prices, with fruits and vegetables projected to rise 2.5-3.5% and 2-3%, respectively. The drought has already led to price increases for certain groceries, including berries, broccoli, and grapes. The Western drought affects over 52 million people, with impacts felt beyond California in states like Texas and Oklahoma.

University of Michigan to screen "American Sniper" despite student objections. The film's depiction of the Iraq War had sparked concerns among some students, but the university cited freedom of expression in its decision to proceed with the screening. An alternative film, "Paddington", will also be shown.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards featured notable moments, including Channing Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez and Amy Schumer's hilarious opening monologue. The show also had its misfires, such as Schumer's archery fail and awkward jokes from presenters. Winners of the night included Kevin Hart and Robert Downey Jr.

Debris from a 20-30ft fiberglass boat, believed to be from the 2011 Japan tsunami, has been towed into an Oregon harbor. The boat fragment contained yellowtail jack fish native to Japanese waters, posing a low ecological threat. The fish will be taken to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

Nigeria marks one-year anniversary of Boko Haram's kidnapping of 276 schoolgirls. Most remain missing, feared raped, brutalized and enslaved, with 50 having escaped soon after abduction. New President Muhammadu Buhari has pledged to combat the militant group.

Easter, a pivotal Christian holiday, marks the culmination of Holy Week and the Easter Triduum, a three-day period of prayer and reflection. The Triduum, spanning Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday, symbolizes the journey from suffering and death to transformation and resurrection. This spiritual progression is a universal human experience, transcending religious boundaries and commercialization.

Kenya has frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters after last week's university massacre. The move is part of a crackdown on the militant group's finances, with more accounts potentially to be frozen. Kenya has also launched airstrikes on Al-Shabaab training camps in Somalia.

Chinese-born entrepreneur Jia Jiang has written a book, "Rejection Proof", detailing his experiences with "100 Days of Rejection", a project where he intentionally sought out rejection to overcome his fear. Jiang's project, which included asking strangers for unusual favors, went viral and led to speaking engagements and job offers. He now aims to help others overcome their own fears of rejection.

US Attorney General Eric Holder has reiterated a ban on Justice Department personnel soliciting prostitutes, citing links to human trafficking. The directive applies even in jurisdictions where prostitution is legal. Violators face suspension or termination, regardless of duty status.

North Carolina authorities investigate possible hate crime after employee Ron Lane, a gay man, was shot and killed at Wayne Community College. Suspect Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, a former work-study program participant, was arrested in Florida after fleeing the scene. Stancil has no prior record, but investigators are looking into potential white supremacist ties.

Amnesty International reports a rise in death sentences worldwide in 2014, with governments increasingly using the death penalty as a tool to combat crime and terrorism. The number of executions recorded globally dropped to 607, but the use of capital punishment remains a concern in countries such as China, Pakistan, and Iran. The trend is seen as a misguided attempt to address security threats, with most countries now abolitionist in law or practice.

Duke University student admits to hanging noose from tree near student union. The student, who is no longer on campus, will face conduct review, while criminal investigations continue. Incident sparks outrage and protests among students and faculty.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known for his role as Leland McKenzie on "L.A. Law", has died at 86. Dysart won an Emmy in 1992 for his portrayal of the character and appeared in every episode of the show. He also had a notable career in film and theatre, with roles in "That Championship Season" and "Wall Street".

Easter celebrations were held worldwide, with Pope Francis leading services at the Vatican and calling for peace in conflict zones. The holiday's date is determined by a combination of lunar phases and the vernal equinox, resulting in varying dates between Western and Orthodox Christians. Easter traditions also include secular symbols like the Easter bunny and colored eggs.

Comedian Chris Rock has sparked conversation on racial profiling after documenting three traffic stops in seven weeks on Twitter. Rock's posts have drawn both support and criticism, with some praising him for highlighting the issue and others accusing him of race-baiting. The incident has reignited discussion on disparities in police treatment of blacks and whites.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died in a car crash in Georgia. Burns, 64, was not wearing a seatbelt when his car hit a tree. He was a founding member of the Southern rock band, leaving in 1975 due to touring exhaustion.

A photo of a cat on stairs has sparked a social media debate over whether it's going up or down. The image, uploaded to Imgur, has gone viral after being shared on 9gag.com. The optical illusion has drawn widespread discussion and attention from advertisers.

US and partners reach framework agreement with Iran to limit nuclear program. The deal, reached in Lausanne, Switzerland, reduces Iran's uranium stockpile and implements strict inspections. Critics are expected to push back against the agreement despite its success in blocking Iran's path to a nuclear weapon.

University of Virginia under investigation for handling of sexual assault cases, with no student ever expelled for such offenses. A retracted Rolling Stone article sparked conversation about campus culture, but its flaws may have set back progress for survivors. Separate investigations by the US Department of Education and a law firm are ongoing.

Indiana Pacers' Chris Copeland stabbed outside NYC nightclub, two Atlanta Hawks players arrested on obstruction charges. Copeland, 31, is in stable condition with knife wounds to elbow and abdomen. Hawks' Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha face charges unrelated to the stabbing incident.

Twisted Sister announces 2016 farewell tour, "Forty and F*ck It", to mark 40th anniversary. The tour will feature new drummer Mike Portnoy, replacing late member A.J. Pero. Two tribute shows will be held in Pero's honor.

John Travolta dismisses HBO's "Going Clear" documentary as negative and based on disgruntled former members. The actor, a longtime Scientologist, praises the church as "brilliant" and credits it with helping him cope with personal tragedy. Travolta has not seen the documentary and says he has no interest in doing so.

"Furious 7" earns record $146 million debut as fans praise emotional tribute to late actor Paul Walker. The film's ending, which retires Walker's character, has left many moviegoers in tears. The tribute features a montage of Walker's scenes set to the song "See You Again".

HBO's "Game of Thrones" premieres its fifth season Sunday, airing in 170 countries simultaneously. The new season is expected to see major story arcs converge, with characters like Tyrion and Daenerys crossing paths. The show's executive producers promise bigger battles and more drama as the series builds towards its conclusion.

Several individuals have survived being stranded at sea for extended periods, including Louis Jordan, who was rescued after 66 days, and Jose Salvador Alvarenga, who survived 13 months adrift in the Pacific. Others, such as Ron Ingraham and Adrian Vasquez, also endured lengthy ordeals before being rescued. These cases highlight the resourcefulness and luck required to survive such extreme situations.

The "Star Wars" saga is being released on digital HD with special features. The features include behind-the-scenes content, such as the creation of sound effects. The collection of the first six films will be available for digital download for the first time.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev found guilty on all 30 counts related to Boston Marathon bombings. Victims and families react with mix of emotions, relief, and gratitude for accountability. Verdict brings sense of closure, but not end to pain and trauma for those affected.

China's former security chief Zhou Yongkang has been formally charged with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets. The 72-year-old is the highest-ranking Chinese Communist Party official to face corruption charges. His case will be tried in Tianjin, with analysts viewing his downfall as a key moment in President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign.

Philadelphia police charge a mother with multiple crimes after she allegedly abandoned her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for four days. The son, who has cerebral palsy, was found with a blanket and Bible, suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and other health issues. The mother was taken into custody in Maryland and will face extradition to Philadelphia.

Walmart's opposition to a religious freedom law in Arkansas has sparked a national debate on gay rights and discrimination. The company's stance, along with criticism from other major businesses, has led to a backlash against similar laws in several states. The issue has also become a focal point in the 2016 presidential campaign.

Pope Francis' humble and inclusive approach has reawakened the faith of a lapsed Catholic. The Pope's tone and actions, such as welcoming gay individuals and serving the poor, have resonated with many who felt rejected by the Church. His leadership has inspired a renewed sense of belonging and spirituality.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and husband Vili Fualaau, who began an affair when he was 13 and she was his 34-year-old teacher, speak out in a new interview. The couple, who will celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary, discuss their marriage and overcoming challenges. Letourneau Fualaau also reveals plans to teach again and have her sex offender status lifted.

Hillary Clinton's presidential candidacy will be a barometer for gender equality in the US, with her win or loss having significant implications for women's political inclusion. A Clinton victory could lead to complacency on women's issues, while a loss could perpetuate myths about women's electability. Her candidacy will be scrutinized through a gender lens, despite partisanship and economic factors being more decisive in presidential elections.

Amnesty International reports a 22% global decrease in executions in 2014, with at least 607 people put to death. However, the number of death sentences handed down increased by 28% to 2,466. The organization criticizes governments for using the death penalty as a tool to tackle perceived security threats.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani has confirmed that the country's Air Self Defense Force has never encountered a UFO from outer space. The statement came in response to a query from lawmaker Antonio Inoki, who asked about the military's response to potential extraterrestrial threats. No evidence of alien visitors has been found, according to Nakatani.

Mark Wahlberg to star in "Patriots' Day", a film about the Boston Marathon bombing. Wahlberg will play Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis, with the film told from his point of view. The project is one of two announced films about the 2013 attack.

Democratic presidential hopefuls Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb appeared together at a dinner in Iowa, showcasing their differing styles. O'Malley worked the crowd with ease, while Webb was more subdued. Both face long odds in their bids, trailing Hillary Clinton in national and state polls.

Nine British citizens, including four children, arrested at Turkey-Syria border for suspected illegal crossing. The group, which included three men and two women, were carrying British passports. Turkish authorities have not disclosed the reason for the attempted crossing.

FedEx has been indicted on 15 counts, including conspiracy and money laundering, for allegedly transporting prescription drugs dispensed with illegal prescriptions. The company argues it is innocent, citing its status as a "common carrier" that cannot be held liable for possessing contraband. The case raises questions about corporate liability and the government's ability to prosecute companies for crimes.

Kenyans mourn 147 victims of Garissa University College terrorist attack. Social media campaign #147notjustanumber shares stories of victims, mostly students, killed by Al-Shabaab. Nation observes emotional Easter services with armed guards in place.

Sweden's parental leave policy allows 480 days off with pay, with 60 days reserved for fathers. A photographer is documenting fathers who take advantage of the policy, showcasing their experiences and challenges. The project aims to promote equal parenting and challenge traditional gender roles.

US President Barack Obama reaffirms commitment to Israel's military advantage over Iran. Obama seeks to reassure Israel amid criticism of nuclear deal with Iran, offering US support in event of attack. Talks on final draft of Iran deal to continue until June 30.

US Religious Freedom Restoration Act sparks controversy amid growing number of state-level laws. Recent court cases have tested the limits of religious freedom, with mixed results for plaintiffs. The law has been used to defend a range of religious practices, from Native American eagle feather ceremonies to Sikh kirpan-wearing.

Five Chinese feminists face up to five years in prison on charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order" over their gender equality campaign. The women were detained in March ahead of International Women's Day and their case has sparked international outcry. Prosecutors must decide by Monday whether to pursue the charges.

Selena's family is creating a hologram-like figure of the late Tejano star, dubbed "Selena the One", which will perform and release new music. The project, using technology from Acrovirt LLC, aims to introduce Selena to new fans and expand her legacy. A tour and new songs are planned for 2018.

Michele Bachmann compares Obama to Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, suggesting his Iran deal will have disastrous consequences. The comment sparked widespread criticism on her Facebook page, with many calling it "moronic" and "despicable". Bachmann has been a vocal opponent of Obama's Iran negotiations.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River" hits theaters, showcasing a decaying Detroit as a backdrop for a post-industrial gothic tale. Gosling's film explores the city's decline and rebirth, highlighting both destruction and resilience. The movie receives a limited release in the US and UK on April 10.

UK man charged with terror offenses after arrest at Luton airport. Yahya Rashid, 19, faces two counts related to preparing and assisting acts of terrorism. He is set to appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Mötley Crüe's Vince Neil botched the US national anthem at a Las Vegas arena football game. The performance drew comparisons to other infamous renditions, including Roseanne Barr's 1990 debacle and Jimi Hendrix's 1969 psychedelic version. Neil's mistake joins a long list of notable anthem flubs.

WWI soldiers' graffiti discovered in underground city near Naours, France, featuring 1,821 names, including Australians, Brits, and Americans. The inscriptions, found in a network of carved-out rooms and pathways, date back to 1916 and provide a human connection to those who fought in the war. Photographer Jeff Gusky has chronicled the site, describing it as a "treasure trove" of historical significance.

The Palestinian Authority has officially joined the International Criminal Court, giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The move, opposed by Israel and the US, paves the way for possible war crimes investigations against Israelis and Palestinians. The ICC will review evidence and determine whether to investigate suspects on both sides.

Anthony Ray Hinton, 58, has been released from Alabama's death row after nearly 30 years. Hinton was convicted of two 1985 murders, but a judge dismissed the charges due to lack of evidence. He maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment, citing racial bias and inadequate legal assistance.

US taxpayers are receiving large refunds, with 8 in 10 getting an average of $3000 back. Simplified tax filing has made the process easier, with many providers offering free services. The refunds have turned Tax Day into a "happy spending spree" for many Americans.

Jordan Spieth maintains 4-shot lead at Masters after 3rd round. Rory McIlroy, Tiger Woods, and Phil Mickelson made moves but failed to significantly close gap. Spieth heads into final round poised for victory despite late double bogey.

NY woman, 39, charged with filing false marriage license application as part of alleged immigration scam. She has been married 10 times, with 9 marriages occurring between 1999 and 2002, and is believed to still be married to 4 men. She faces up to 4 years in prison if convicted.

Indiana pizzeria at center of controversy over refusal to cater same-sex wedding, sparking boycotts and death threats. Despite backlash, supporters raise over $842,000 for the business through a GoFundMe campaign. The incident highlights divisive debate over state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

Mindy Kaling's brother Vijay Chokalingam has revealed he pretended to be African-American to gain admission to medical school, sparking controversy over affirmative action. Chokalingam's scheme, which he claims proves unfair advantages for minority applicants, has been met with criticism and accusations of racism. He is now writing a book about his experiences, titled "Almost Black".

Antarctica records possible all-time high temperature of 63.5F. The reading, taken at Argentina's Esperanza Base, is being verified by the World Meteorological Organization. A final determination is expected by late summer or early fall.

US officials have backed away from a spring timeline for an Iraqi-led assault on Mosul, saying a potential invasion may be soon or sometime in the future. The city, a key stronghold of ISIS, is considered a complex and challenging target. Airstrikes have already begun to soften up ISIS positions in the area.

Paddy Power has deleted a tweet that made a controversial reference to police killings of unarmed African-American men. The Irish betting company had used the tweet to promote a piece on Liverpool vs. Newcastle United match statistics. The company has apologized, stating that no offense was meant.

Philadelphia police have added attempted murder to charges against Nyia Parler, 41, who allegedly left her quadriplegic son in the woods for days. Parler is currently in custody in Maryland, where she is undergoing unspecified treatment before extradition to Philadelphia. She faces multiple charges, including aggravated assault and reckless endangerment.

South Korean man Kim Ki-Jong charged with attempted murder for stabbing US Ambassador Mark Lippert. Kim, 55, also faces charges of assaulting a foreign envoy and business obstruction. His trial must begin within 14 days of indictment.

Jill Duggar Dillard, star of "19 Kids and Counting", gives birth to 9lb 10oz son Israel David. The baby arrived over a week past due date. Dillard and husband Derick announced the birth via her parents' Facebook page.

"Furious 7" is poised for a record-breaking $135-138 million opening weekend in North America. The film, the final one featuring the late Paul Walker, is projected to earn nearly $300 million worldwide by Easter Sunday. It will be playing in a record 4,003 domestic theaters and over 10,500 international screens.

Secret Service supervisor Xavier Morales placed on leave amid allegations of sexual assault against a female employee. Morales allegedly made unwanted advances at a party and later tried to kiss the woman in the office. The incident is the latest scandal to hit the agency, which has faced numerous controversies in recent months.

Hillary Clinton has announced her candidacy for the 2016 US presidential election, bringing extensive experience and skills to the table. Despite her strengths, Clinton faces challenges including doubts about her authenticity and potential liabilities such as her husband's involvement and gender bias. A successful campaign will depend on her ability to connect with voters and articulate a compelling vision for the White House.

The US Department of Justice will begin negotiating with Ferguson, Missouri, to restructure its police department, which has been accused of racial discrimination. The city has seen significant changes in recent weeks, including the resignation of its police chief and town manager, and the election of two new black city council members. The DOJ's negotiations will determine the scope of reforms, which could include disbanding the police department or implementing regional policing integration.

Etihad Airways has lost a 2-year-old cat, Felix, belonging to an American couple after a flight from Abu Dhabi to New York's JFK Airport. The cat's carrier was damaged, allowing it to escape, and despite an ongoing search, Felix remains missing. Etihad Airways is investigating and working to locate the cat, reviewing its pet handling procedures in the wake of the incident.

Louis Jordan, 37, rescued after 66 days adrift in Atlantic Ocean. Jordan, an inexperienced sailor, survived on fish and collected rainwater after his sailboat capsized in a storm. He was found in surprisingly good condition by the crew of a container ship.
